evals.prompt: My React app has src/components/ with 180 files, src/hooks/ with 60, and src/utils/ with 40 — all flat. Every PR review argues about where new files go. Restructure it.
evals.expected_output: Refuses to move anything immediately. First verifies a green build/test baseline, inventories the tree (hot files, external consumers, path-bearing configs), then proposes a feature-first target (src/features/<name>/ with colocated components/hooks/tests, src/components/ reserved for domain-free design-system UI, utils dissolved into content-named lib/ modules). Produces an old-to-new mapping table sliced into stages, and stops at an approval gate before executing. Each stage ends green and committed; move commits contain no behavior changes.

evals.prompt: I'm starting a new Go service (HTTP API + a queue worker, one team, maybe 10k lines eventually). How should I lay out the folders? Should I follow golang-standards/project-layout?
evals.expected_output: Recommends starting small and structuring at pain: cmd/server and cmd/worker with thin main.go files since there are two binaries, everything else private-by-default under internal/ as feature-named packages (payments.Process style, no util/common/models packages — the package name is the API prefix). Notes pkg/ has no compiler semantics and is usually unnecessary, and that golang-standards/project-layout is a community template, not official Go guidance — the official go.dev module-organization docs are the reference to verify against. Flags that import cycles are compiler-enforced so dependency direction must be designed up front.

evals.prompt: Our Python FastAPI service is a flat package at the repo root with routers/, schemas/, services/ folders and a giant utils.py. We also run celery. Should we move to src layout, and how do we do it without breaking prod?
evals.expected_output: Yes: src layout so tests exercise the installed package instead of the checkout, with pyproject.toml as the single packaging source and tests/ outside the package. Restructures the layer bins (routers/schemas/services) into feature-first packages and dissolves utils.py into content-named lib modules. Requires absolute imports throughout. Critically, censuses dotted-path strings before moving: the uvicorn/gunicorn app target, celery include lists and task names (moving a module renames its tasks — pin explicit names or drain queues first), entry points in pyproject, settings modules. Migration is staged with a green verify loop per stage including a runtime smoke (boot the app, start a worker), since unit tests do not catch broken dotted paths.

evals.prompt: We have three Node repos (web, api, worker) that copy-paste the same domain types and API client between them, and they keep drifting. Consolidate them into a monorepo?
evals.expected_output: Confirms the drift is exactly the monorepo signal, then plans two strictly ordered migrations: first import each repo with full git history preserved into apps/<name> as-is and verify each still builds (Dockerfile/CI paths changed — census sweep); only then restructure stage by stage, extracting the duplicated types and client into packages/ (workspace-declared dependencies, no ../../ cross-package imports, no dependency cycle, apps never imported). Warns that the drifted copies differ, so diffing them comes first and genuinely divergent logic is behavior work for code-implementation, not silent unification. CI consolidation with paths filters is its own stage.

evals.prompt: Last month someone reorganized our repo's folders. Tests were green, PR looked fine, but two weeks later we found CI had stopped running half the test suite and a deploy broke. We're about to do another reorg — how do we make sure file moves don't silently break things this time?
evals.expected_output: Explains the silent-breaker problem: typecheckers catch broken imports but nothing catches broken strings. Prescribes a path-bearing census built before the plan and grepped after every stage: CI workflow paths: filters (a moved folder silently stops triggering workflows — the exact failure described), CODEOWNERS patterns, Dockerfile COPY paths, coverage/lint globs, dotted-path strings, docs. Each stage uses git mv with moves-plus-mechanical-fixes-only commits (history/rename detection preserved), tool-driven import fixes verified by the typechecker, a grep sweep for old paths, and a runtime smoke when entry points moved. Never batch stages; each stage green and committed as a rollback point.

evals.prompt: While you're moving our files into the new folder structure, can you also rename the badly named functions and clean up that gross date-parsing logic in the files you touch? Saves us a second pass.
evals.expected_output: Declines to mix the two, explaining why rather than just citing a rule: git detects renames by content similarity, so a commit that moves and rewrites a file destroys git log --follow history and blame, and behavior changes hide unreviewably inside a 300-file move diff. Move commits stay moves plus mechanical path fixes only. Offers the correct sequencing instead: finish the restructure stages green, then do symbol renames and the date-parsing cleanup as separate follow-up commits/PRs through the code-implementation workflow, listing the requested cleanups as follow-up work in the plan so they are not lost.

evals.prompt: Our NestJS backend grew organically — controllers and services are scattered everywhere, some in src/api/, some in src/logic/. What target structure should we migrate to and how?
evals.expected_output: Hands the target layout to nestjs-dev-guidelines (01-folder-structure, 03-module-design: src/{core,common,integrations,modules,events,commands} with one module per bounded context) rather than inventing a competing NestJS layout, then supplies the migration machinery from this skill: green verify baseline, inventory, old-to-new mapping table covering every file, staged execution with approval before the first move, per-stage green commits, and the path-bearing census (CI filters, Dockerfile, configs).
